entities.name: Zapatista Army of National Liberation
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Zapatista Army of National Liberation (EZLN), founded on January 1, 1994, emerged as a significant revolutionary group in Chiapas, Mexico, advocating for indigenous rights and social justice in the face of neoliberal economic policies. The group gained international attention with their armed uprising against the Mexican government, coinciding with the implementation of the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA). Led by the charismatic figure Subcomandante Marcos, the Zapatistas utilized a combination of guerrilla tactics and political advocacy to highlight the struggles of the indigenous population while challenging the broader socio-economic disparities in Mexico.

Key events surrounding the Zapatista movement include the 1994 uprising in San Cristóbal de las Casas, where the EZLN seized towns, demanding land reform and autonomy for indigenous communities. The conflict drew widespread media coverage, prompting global solidarity movements and discussions about indigenous rights, economic justice, and anti-globalization. The Zapatistas declared war on the Mexican state, yet they also engaged in negotiations, culminating in the San Andrés Accords of 1996, which aimed to address indigenous rights and autonomy, though implementation has been uneven.

The legacy of the Zapatista Army extends beyond the confines of Chiapas, influencing various social movements across Latin America and the globe. Their innovative use of the internet to spread their message and connect with activists worldwide established a model for modern grassroots organizing. The Zapatistas' emphasis on democracy, autonomy, and self-governance continues to resonate, inspiring new generations of activists who challenge systemic inequalities in both local and global contexts.
